section.title: Be Strong and Courageous
section.sectionRationale: The book opens in the gap left by a death. Moses, the servant through whom God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave the law, is gone, and a new leader stands on the edge of the promised land with a task too large for any man. Into that silence the LORD speaks, commissioning Joshua, renewing the ancient promise of the land, and pressing home one command four times over: be strong and courageous. It is one tight movement, the divine charge that launches the whole conquest.
section.thesis: The land is God's gift and God's oath, not Joshua's achievement; so the courage Joshua is commanded to have rests not on his own strength but on the presence of the LORD who never leaves him and on the word of the LORD he is to meditate on day and night.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the commission after Moses' death, verses 1 to 2; the promise of land and unfailing presence, verses 3 to 5; and the fourfold call to strong, courageous obedience anchored in the Book of the Law, verses 6 to 9.

units.label: The commission after Moses' death
units.note: Moses My servant is dead; now arise

verses.text: Now after the death of His servant Moses, the LORD spoke to {{yehoshua|Joshua}} son of Nun, Moses’ assistant, saying,
“Moses My servant is dead. Now therefore arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan into the land that I am giving to the children of Israel.

units.label: The promise of land and unfailing presence
units.note: I will never leave you nor forsake you

verses.text: I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread, just as I promised to Moses.
Your territory shall extend from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and west as far as the Great Sea.
No one shall stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so will I be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you.

units.label: The fourfold call to courage and obedience
units.note: be strong and courageous; meditate on the Law

verses.text: Be {{chazaq|strong}} and {{amats|courageous}}, for you shall give these people the {{nachalah|inheritance}} of the land that I swore to their fathers I would give them.

Above all, be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe all the {{torah|law}} that My servant Moses commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may prosper wherever you go.

This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; {{hagah|meditate}} on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. For then you will prosper and succeed in all you do.
Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”

yehoshua.gloss: Joshua, meaning the LORD saves or the LORD is salvation. Moses renamed Hoshea son of Nun to Yehoshua, Numbers 13:16. It is the same name, in its later Greek form Iesous, that the angel gives to Mary's son, Matthew 1:21; the leader who brings Israel into the land bears the very name of the greater Savior who brings His people into eternal rest.

chazaq.gloss: To be strong, firm, resolute; to take hold and hold fast. Repeated with amats as a paired command, it is the charge sounded four times over Joshua. The strength called for is not raw self-confidence but a firm grip on God's promise and God's word in the face of an overwhelming task.

amats.gloss: To be courageous, bold, alert; to steel oneself. Paired with chazaq throughout the charge, it summons a courage grounded not in Joshua's ability but in the assurance that the LORD goes with him and will not fail him.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, possession, allotted heritage. The land is Israel's nachalah because it is a gift handed down by promise, sworn to the fathers, not seized by right. The word governs the whole book: chapters 13 to 21 divide this inheritance tribe by tribe, and the New Testament lifts the idea to the imperishable inheritance kept in heaven, 1 Peter 1:4.

torah.gloss: Law, instruction, teaching. The Book of the Law, the covenant word given through Moses, is to shape everything Joshua does. Success in Canaan is tied not to military genius but to careful, wholehearted obedience to God's revealed word, turning aside neither to the right nor the left.

hagah.gloss: To meditate, mutter, murmur; to ponder something by speaking it under one's breath. To meditate on the Law day and night is to keep God's word constantly on the lips and in the mind, the same picture that opens Psalm 1. It is not idle reflection but the steady, spoken rehearsing of God's word that produces obedience.

basic.context: Moses is dead, and Joshua, his long-time assistant, must lead a whole nation across the Jordan into a land full of fortified cities and strong peoples. The task is impossible on paper. So God speaks. He does not hand Joshua a battle plan; He gives him a promise and a command. The promise: I am giving you this land, and I will be with you as I was with Moses, and I will never leave you. The command, sounded four times, is the same: be strong and courageous. The key question the passage answers is: where does courage for an overwhelming calling actually come from?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that opens a book of conquest. The land promise here is specific to Israel and to Joshua's moment; we should not read every detail as a direct promise of real estate to us. Yet the New Testament deliberately takes God's words to Joshua, I will never leave you nor forsake you, and applies them to every believer, Hebrews 13:5. The abiding truth is that God commands courageous obedience and grounds it in His own faithful presence and His word, not in our strength.
basic.originalLanguages: The new leader is Yehoshua, the LORD saves, the very name later given to Jesus. The paired command chazaq and amats, be strong and be courageous, rings out four times. The land is Israel's nachalah, its inheritance by promise. And the secret to success is not the sword but the torah, God's word, which Joshua is to hagah, to meditate on, day and night.
basic.typology: Joshua stepping into Moses' place to lead God's people into the promised land foreshadows Christ, who takes us beyond what the law through Moses could do and leads His people into the true rest. The land itself, the inheritance, is a shadow of the eternal inheritance secured in Christ. The word that must never depart from Joshua's mouth points to Christ, the Word made flesh.
basic.christ: Joshua bears the name that Jesus would bear, the LORD saves. Where Joshua led one generation into a land they would eventually lose, Jesus leads all His people into a rest they can never lose, Hebrews 4:8-9. The command be strong and courageous, grounded in God's presence, finds its deepest yes in Christ, who is Immanuel, God with us, and who promises, I am with you always.
basic.god: God is the giver: the land is His to give, sworn by oath to the fathers, so the whole enterprise rests on His faithfulness, not Israel's merit. He is present: I will be with you, I will never leave you nor forsake you. And He is the God who speaks, binding His people's flourishing to obedience to His word. Courage is commanded because the God who commands it goes with the one He sends.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 31 records Moses charging Joshua with the same words before he dies. Psalm 1 pictures the blessed one who meditates on God's law day and night. Hebrews 13 lifts I will never leave you nor forsake you into a promise for every Christian. And Hebrews 4 shows that Joshua's rest was only a shadow of the rest we have in Christ.
basic.oneStory: The promise of land made to Abraham now moves toward fulfillment as a new leader named the LORD saves stands ready to bring Israel in. God's presence and word, not human strength, will win it. The whole scene points beyond Canaan to the greater Joshua, Jesus, who leads His people into the rest that lasts forever.

context.literary:
The commissioning follows a recognizable Old Testament pattern also seen in Moses' own call at the burning bush and Gideon's call in Judges 6, a crisis of leadership, a divine address naming the task, a promise of presence, and a command to act. What marks this scene as distinct is its density of repetition; the fourfold be strong and courageous, verses 6, 7, and 9, and again in verse 18, functions almost as a chorus binding the whole chapter together, so that whatever else changes between the divine speech of verses 1-9 and the human response of verses 10-18, that one command recurs untouched.

The speech itself moves through three registers. Verses 1-2 are almost entirely announcement, a death reported and a new name summoned; verses 3-5 shift into covenant language borrowed wholesale from Deuteronomy, every place the sole of your foot will tread echoing Deuteronomy 11:24 nearly word for word; and verses 6-9 turn to direct command, framed by an inclusio, be strong and courageous opening the section and the LORD your God is with you wherever you go closing it. Structurally, then, the passage argues before it commands, three verses of promise earn three verses of imperative.

The chapter is also framed as pure divine speech with almost no narrated action; Joshua himself says nothing here, and does not move until verse 10. The commissioning is complete in words alone, before a single step is taken toward the river.
context.historical:
Joshua had already stood on this same ground once before, forty years earlier, as one of the twelve men Moses sent to scout Canaan, and one of only two who returned urging Israel to go up and take the land at once, Numbers 13-14. That entire generation of adults died in the wilderness for refusing to trust that report, so the man now being commissioned is himself a living witness against the unbelief this new charge is meant to overcome; it is not an accident that be strong and courageous is put in the mouth of one who once said exactly that to a nation that would not listen.

The land grant language of verses 3-4, I have given you every place, matches the form of ancient royal land grants documented across the ancient Near East, where a sovereign transferred territory to a loyal servant with a formula of gift rather than negotiation; Israel's possession of Canaan is cast in the same shape, land given by a greater King rather than territory earned by conquest, even though real fighting still lay ahead. The territorial description, from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates and west to the Great Sea, marks the outer, ideal limit of the promise first given to Abraham, Genesis 15:18, a border Israel would only briefly approach under David and Solomon, 1 Kings 4:21, and never permanently hold.
context.canonical:
This commissioning deliberately reuses Deuteronomy 31:6-8, where Moses himself first spoke be strong and courageous over Joshua and the whole nation before he died, so that Joshua 1 functions less as a new revelation than as God's own ratification, in his own voice, of what his servant had already said; the human handoff of chapter 34 needed a matching divine handoff here to be complete.

The chapter also sits inside a family of biblical commissioning scenes, Moses at the bush, Gideon in Judges 6, Isaiah in the temple, Jeremiah as a boy, each answered by fear and each met with a promise of divine presence rather than a resume of the candidate's qualifications; Joshua's charge follows the same shape, though unusually for the pattern, Joshua himself raises no recorded objection, unlike Moses' excuses or Jeremiah's protest that he is too young.

Its emphasis on meditating on the Book of the Law day and night is picked up almost verbatim by Psalm 1:2, whose blessed man delights in the law of the LORD and meditates on it day and night, suggesting that Joshua's charge as a leader became, in time, a pattern held out to every individual believer, not only to the one commissioned to conquer a land. And its central promise, I will never leave you nor forsake you, is lifted directly into Hebrews 13:5, addressed no longer to one man crossing one river but to every reader facing any circumstance at all.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The narrator wants Israel's first readers, themselves later inheritors of this same land and this same book of the law, to see their own security modeled in Joshua's commissioning rather than assume it belonged only to him. Every reason given for courage is something true about God, not something true about Joshua's resume, so that a reader with far less standing than Joshua, Moses' own attendant for decades, could still find equal ground for courage in the same unchanging presence and the same available word. The author also intends a specific correction, this generation must succeed where their parents failed at Kadesh Barnea, and the charge to observe all the law, turning neither right nor left, functions as the antidote to the unbelief that kept an entire generation out of the land the first time the border was this close. Courage here is not a feeling to work up but a settled decision to keep obeying what has already been spoken, regardless of the size of the task ahead.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The land grant itself, and its precise ancient borders from the Euphrates to the Great Sea, described one specific, historical transfer of territory to one specific nation at one moment in redemptive history; nothing here promises modern readers real estate, a job, or a particular outcome for reading their Bibles. What is prescriptive, and what the New Testament itself treats as prescriptive by quoting it directly, is the pattern of courage grounded in presence rather than resources, and of success measured by careful, wholehearted obedience to God's revealed word rather than by circumstance. Even the promise you will prosper and succeed describes covenant faithfulness bearing its intended fruit within God's own redemptive plan for Joshua's generation, not a guarantee detachable from obedience and applied to any reader's private ambitions.

debates.question: Is the promise you will prosper and succeed a guarantee of worldly success for believers who read the Bible?

views.label: A covenant promise tied to obedience, not a prosperity formula
views.case: The prospering promised to Joshua is explicitly bound to careful obedience to the whole Law and to the covenant task God gave him; it is God's faithfulness to His own promise about the land, not a general pledge that Bible reading yields wealth or ease. Read in context, and alongside the suffering of faithful people throughout Scripture, it cannot be turned into a success formula.

views.label: A principle that God blesses obedience, rightly qualified
views.case: There is a real and abiding principle that God honors those who treasure and obey His word, and that a life shaped by Scripture is a flourishing life in the deepest sense. The danger is only in flattening that into guaranteed material prosperity; understood as the true flourishing of covenant faithfulness, the promise still speaks.

debates.bearing: Both guard against a prosperity-gospel misreading, the text ties blessing to wholehearted obedience within God's redemptive purpose, and Scripture's own witness shows that faithfulness often costs, even as God remains present and good.

debates.question: Are the borders named in verse 4, from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates, meant as a literal, achievable territorial claim?

views.label: A real, if largely unrealized, historical claim
views.case: The same outer border is promised to Abraham in Genesis 15:18 and briefly approached under Solomon, whose influence is said to reach from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, 1 Kings 4:21, suggesting the language describes an actual, if rarely occupied, territorial ceiling rather than pure metaphor.

views.label: An idealized covenantal horizon
views.case: Israel never continuously controlled anything like this full territory even at its historical peak, and ancient royal land grants regularly used maximal, rhetorically total language to express the completeness of a gift rather than a strict property line, so the description functions more as a statement that the gift is whole and unqualified than as a literal map.

debates.bearing: Either way, the text's own point is God's totality of gift rather than Israel's guaranteed occupation of every named mile, since even the fullest historical extent under Solomon was temporary and partial.

study.originalLanguages:
Joshua is introduced in verse 1 as Moses' assistant, a title used elsewhere of young Samuel ministering before the LORD, 1 Samuel 3:1, and of the sanctuary service of the Levites, so that Joshua's decades beside Moses are cast less as an apprenticeship in leadership technique than as a kind of priestly attendance, watching and serving before he is ever asked to lead.

Verse 3's promise, every place the sole of your foot will tread, borrows a fixed Hebrew idiom, the sole of the foot, from Deuteronomy 11:24, but it also stands in silent contrast to an earlier scene using the same idiom in reverse, after the flood, Noah's dove found no place to rest her foot and returned to the ark, Genesis 8:9. Where the dove could find no resting ground anywhere in a ruined world, Israel is promised ground to stand on everywhere she goes, an old idiom turned from lost rest to given rest.

The promise I will never leave you nor forsake you, verse 5, pairs two verbs, one common, to leave, and one rarer, literally to slacken or let the hand drop. The same root gives the command be still in Psalm 46:10, more literally let your hands fall, and know that I am God, so that the God who tells anxious nations to drop their weapons and be still is the same God who promises Joshua he will never let his own grip on him go slack.

The second occurrence of the charge, verse 7, alone adds the intensifier very, be strong and very courageous, precisely at the point where the topic shifts from military conquest to obedience to the whole law; the text seems to regard covenant faithfulness, turning neither right nor left, as requiring even more resolve than the battles ahead.

Twice more the chapter reaches for set Deuteronomic phrases, turn not to the right or to the left, verse 7, the exact idiom Moses used for covenant faithfulness in Deuteronomy 5:32, 17:11, and 28:14, and meditate on it day and night, verse 8, a fixed merism for constant, unbroken attention, the same phrase Psalm 1:2 later uses of the blessed man's delight in the law. Joshua's charge, in other words, is built almost entirely from Moses' own vocabulary, so that even its wording insists the mantle has genuinely passed rather than begun something new.

typology.type: Joshua, the LORD saves, succeeding Moses to lead Israel across the Jordan into the land, verses 1-2
typology.fulfillment: Joshua's own name already preaches a gospel before the conquest begins a single battle, he leads not by his own strength but by bearing a name that confesses whose work this really is. The angel gives that very name, in its Greek form, to Mary's son precisely because he will save his people from their sins, Matthew 1:21, so the correspondence runs deeper than a shared sound; both leaders bring God's people out of one condition and into another, though Joshua's crossing still left Israel exposed to conquest and later exile, while the greater Joshua's crossing through death secures an inheritance no army can ever take back.

typology.type: The land, given as Israel's inheritance, sworn by oath rather than earned by strength, verses 2-6
typology.fulfillment: Every acre named here would eventually be lost, first to Assyria and then to Babylon, proving that this inheritance, however sure the oath behind it, was never built to last forever. Peter describes a better inheritance kept in heaven for believers, imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, 1 Peter 1:4, precisely because it does not depend on continued military possession of any hillside, the escalation running from a gift that could be lost by unfaithfulness to a gift that cannot be lost at all.

typology.type: The Book of the Law that must never depart from Joshua's mouth, meditated on day and night, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: Success here is tied to keeping God's spoken word constantly close, a discipline of the mouth and the mind rather than a private feeling. John says the Word itself became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:14, and Paul tells believers to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly, Colossians 3:16, so that what Joshua kept on his lips as a scroll, the church is called to carry as a living relationship with the Word himself.

study.christ:
The name itself is doing theology before the narrative does. Joshua's name means the LORD saves, and it is precisely this name, in its Greek form, that the angel instructs Joseph to give Mary's son, because he will save his people from their sins, Matthew 1:21. But the correspondence is not simple repetition. The first Joshua saves by leading an army across a flooded river and by the edge of a sword; the second saves by going down into death himself and coming up on the other side of it, so that the very shape of the salvation each name announces has changed even while the name has not.

Hebrews builds a careful argument on exactly this difference. If Joshua had actually given God's people the rest he was commissioned to bring, David would have had no reason to keep speaking, generations later, of another day still called today, warning against hardened hearts, Hebrews 4:6-8. Since Scripture keeps that appeal open long after Joshua's own conquest was finished, a further rest must remain for God's people, a rest Hebrews locates in Jesus rather than in any further stretch of territory, Hebrews 4:9-10.

The covenant promise underneath Joshua's courage, that the LORD would never leave him nor forsake him, verse 5, is not retired once Joshua dies; Hebrews quotes it as a standing word to any believer facing want or fear, Hebrews 13:5-6, and the risen Jesus makes almost the identical promise his own parting word, teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you, and surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age, Matthew 28:19-20, deliberately echoing the very charge Joshua once received.

Caution belongs here too. Not every detail, the Jordan's flood stage or Joshua's specific itinerary, is a coded picture of the gospel; the passage is first a real commissioning of a real leader for a real war. What the New Testament itself licenses is the trajectory from a name, a rest, and a promise of presence, all first spoken over Joshua, to their fuller and final form in Jesus.
study.god:
This scene shows God speaking into a specific kind of silence, the silence that follows a death, and choosing to fill it immediately rather than let the nation sit leaderless even for a chapter. That timing itself says something about his character, he does not wait to be asked before providing what his people need next, and the very first word out of his mouth, after naming Moses' death, is arise, an immediate call back into forward motion rather than an invitation to prolonged mourning.

He grounds every command in something true about himself rather than in Joshua's resume. As I was with Moses, so will I be with you, verse 5, ties Joshua's future entirely to a past already proven; the God being trusted here is not an unknown quantity being tested for the first time but the same God whose faithfulness through forty wilderness years, plagues, a parted sea, daily bread, is already public record. Courage commanded without that history behind it would be presumption; commanded with it, it is simple realism about who God has already shown himself to be.

He also binds his people's flourishing to their attention to his word rather than to their own cleverness or force. Meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it, verse 8, makes obedience, not strategy, the stated condition of success, a striking claim to make to a man about to lead a military campaign against fortified cities. And he repeats himself, four times in nine verses the same command lands, be strong and courageous, not because Joshua is slow to understand but because fear does not usually yield to being told once; God's patience with a frightened servant is itself a small, easily missed feature of who he is here.

For worship, the passage teaches that courage is a response to a character already revealed rather than a feeling summoned from nowhere, and that the God who speaks after a death is the same God still speaking into whatever silence a reader is facing now.

crossReferences.note: Moses had already spoken nearly this exact charge over Joshua and the whole assembly before he died, be strong and courageous, do not be afraid, for the LORD your God goes with you, so that God's word to Joshua here functions as his own personal ratification, in his own voice, of what his dying servant had already promised on his behalf.

Forty years earlier Joshua himself had urged Israel to go up and take the land at once, trusting God's presence, while the rest of that generation refused out of fear and died in the wilderness for it; the man commanding courage in chapter 1 is the same man once shouted down for having exactly this courage first.

The blessed man of the psalm delights in the law of the LORD and meditates on it day and night, and like a tree planted by streams of water, prospers in all he does, applying to any reader the discipline first laid specifically on a nation's military commander.

Isaiah promises a fearful, exiled nation almost this same combination of words, do not fear, I am with you, I will strengthen and help you, showing that the presence promised to one leader before one campaign becomes, centuries later, a comfort spoken to a whole defeated people facing a very different kind of return.

The writer quotes God's promise to Joshua word for word, I will never leave you nor forsake you, and applies it not to a nation crossing a river but to any believer's contentment and freedom from the fear of what people can do.

Because Scripture keeps urging God's people toward rest long after Joshua's own conquest ended, the writer argues that Joshua's crossing could not have been the final rest God intended, and that a further Sabbath rest still remains for God's people in Christ.

The risen Jesus, having received all authority, commissions his followers with a task, teach them to obey everything I have commanded, and a promise, I am with you always, deliberately recalling the shape, though not the wording, of God's charge to Joshua before an earlier crossing.

The territorial description of verse 4, from the wilderness to the Euphrates, repeats almost exactly the outer border of the land God first swore to Abraham centuries earlier, showing this commissioning as the long-delayed activation of a promise rather than a fresh grant.

study.oneStory:
Genesis had already sworn this land to Abraham, and Numbers had already brought one generation to its very border and watched them refuse it out of fear, so that this chapter opens with the promise of land older than Israel's nationhood and a fear of that same land recent enough that everyone listening had buried parents who died because of it. The charge to be strong and courageous is not generic encouragement; it is God's specific answer to a specific, recently repeated failure.

What follows in the rest of Joshua shows this charge partly succeeding and partly not. The conquest does happen, largely as promised, yet the book itself records incomplete obedience almost immediately, Achan's theft in chapter 7, and unconquered pockets of land still listed at Joshua's own death, chapter 13. Israel's later history under the judges and the kings shows a nation that could take a land yet still lose its heart, ending eventually in the very exile this promise seemed to make unthinkable.

The unresolved thread the book of Joshua leaves behind, a real but incomplete rest, a real but temporary land, is exactly what Hebrews later names and answers, arguing that another rest must remain because this one, however genuine, was never final, Hebrews 4:8-9. The whole scene therefore sits inside the Bible's longer story as one more chapter still waiting for its ending, God's ancient promise to Abraham, God's fresh charge to Joshua, Israel's mixed record of courage and failure across the centuries that follow, and finally the greater Joshua who succeeds where every earlier crossing eventually came up short, leading his people not merely into a land but into the very presence of God, where no further conquest or exile can ever undo what has been given.

quiz.q: What command does God repeat to Joshua throughout this passage?

options.text: Be strong and courageous, grounded in God's presence and word.
options.note: The charge sounds four times and is anchored in the LORD being with him wherever he goes.

options.text: Prepare your weapons and train the army for battle.
options.note: Israel will fight, but God's actual repeated command is about courage and obedience, not military preparation.

options.text: Choose capable officers to share the leadership burden.
options.note: Delegation appears elsewhere in Moses' story; here God's repeated word is be strong and courageous.

options.text: Wait quietly and do nothing until the enemy attacks.
options.note: God commands Joshua to arise and cross over, the opposite of passivity.

quiz.q: On what does God ground the courage He commands?

options.text: On His own unfailing presence: I will never leave you nor forsake you.
options.note: Verse 5 and verse 9 root the courage in God's presence, not Joshua's ability.

options.text: On the promise that Joshua will meditate on the Law and obey it.
options.note: Obedience to the word is central, but the deepest ground given for courage is God's presence with him.

options.text: On Joshua's proven skill as Moses' assistant.
options.note: Joshua's experience is real, but the text grounds courage in God, not in Joshua's resume.

options.text: On the weakness of the peoples living in Canaan.
options.note: Canaan's peoples were strong and fortified; the ground of courage is God's presence, not their weakness.

quiz.q: How is Joshua to relate to the Book of the Law?

options.text: It must not depart from his mouth; he is to meditate on it day and night and carefully obey it.
options.note: Verse 8 ties his success to constant meditation on and obedience to God's word.

options.text: He should read it once before crossing the Jordan.
options.note: He is to know it, but the command is continual, day and night, not a single reading.

options.text: He should keep it stored safely in the ark and consult the priests.
options.note: The Law was kept by the ark, but Joshua is personally to meditate on it constantly.

options.text: He may set it aside now that Moses is gone.
options.note: The opposite: the word Moses gave is to govern everything Joshua does.

quiz.q: Why is the land called Israel's inheritance rather than something they earned?

options.text: Because God is giving it as a gift, sworn by oath to their fathers.
options.note: Verses 2 to 6 present the land as God's sworn gift, an inheritance, not a wage.

options.text: Because Israel's obedience in the wilderness had earned it.
options.note: Obedience matters, but the land is grounded in God's oath, not Israel's merit; that generation had actually failed.

options.text: Because they were the strongest nation in the region.
options.note: Israel was not the strongest; the land is a gift by promise, not a spoil of superior power.

options.text: Because they had purchased it from the Canaanites.
options.note: There is no purchase; the land is God's to give and He gives it by oath.

quiz.q: How does Joshua point forward to Jesus?

options.text: He bears the name the LORD saves and leads God's people into the inheritance, foreshadowing Jesus who leads His people into lasting rest.
options.note: Joshua and Jesus share a name and a role; Hebrews 4 shows Joshua's rest was a shadow of Christ's.

options.text: He shows that a strong human leader is all God's people really need.
options.note: Joshua leads well, but the passage roots everything in God; the greater Joshua is Christ, not merely a strong man.

options.text: He proves that the promised land is the final goal of salvation.
options.note: Canaan is a shadow; the true inheritance and rest are found in Christ, not in the land itself.

options.text: He has no real connection to Jesus.
options.note: The shared name and the pattern of leading God's people into rest clearly point to Christ.

questions: God commanded courage but grounded it in His presence, not in Joshua's ability. Where are you being called to be strong and courageous, and how would it change things to lean on God's presence rather than your own resources?
Joshua was to meditate on God's word day and night. What would it look like for Scripture to be that constantly on your lips and mind this week?
The land was a gift, an inheritance sworn by God, not something Israel earned. How does receiving your standing with God as gift rather than achievement free you to obey Him?
God's promise to Joshua, I will never leave you nor forsake you, is spoken to every believer in Hebrews 13. How does that promise steady you in the task or fear you are facing right now?

Joshua bore the name the LORD saves and led one generation into a land they would lose; Jesus leads His people into a rest they can never lose. How does knowing the greater Joshua change the way you face your calling?

translationNotes.note: The Great Sea is the Mediterranean, as the BSB footnote notes.
The promise I will never leave you nor forsake you is marked in the BSB as cited in Hebrews 13:5, where it is applied to all believers.
Joshua son of Nun is Yehoshua, the LORD saves; Moses had renamed him from Hoshea, Numbers 13:16. The name is the same one later given to Jesus.
